prize_parts.citation: for the invention and realisation of optical lattice clocks based on magic-wavelength trapping of neutral atoms

statement.case_for: My preferred configuration is unchanged from round 1: a single-achievement prize for optical lattice clocks, credited to Katori and Ye. The scientific case is one I can state as a mechanism. At the magic wavelength the differential light shift of the clock transition vanishes to first order, so many atoms can be confined in the Lamb-Dicke regime, with Doppler and recoil shifts suppressed, while quantum projection noise falls with the atom number. Katori proposed the idea and Ye's group drove the scheme to systematic uncertainties near 1e-18 and used it for gravitational-redshift and many-body clock physics. Several independent laboratories agree with each other at that level. Having read the whole round-1 exchange, I note that six members prefer B014 and that the two who do not, Danielsson and Eriksson, both call it the cleaner attribution. I do not count that as evidence in itself, and I discount it, because the chair's file shows some positions moved toward B014 after the opening ballots. What persuades me is that the reasons given in the individual files are independent of each other (mechanism, reproducibility, compact credit), and that none of the files disputes the physics. In response to the chair's question, the citation can carry the distinction from the 2005 and 2012 prizes in one sentence, by naming the invention, magic-wavelength trapping of neutral atoms, and not precision time in general.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation remains that this is a precision-measurement invention in a lineage already prized in 1989, 2005 and 2012, so a critic can call it an incremental successor. I think the mechanism answers that, but the judgement is not free of doubt. A second reservation is attribution. Lemonde, Lisdat, Ludlow, Takamoto and the ion-clock groups lie outside the two names, and I have not verified priority dates myself. Katori's magic-wavelength proposal around 2001-2003 preceding the strontium lattice demonstrations is what Lindroth and Johansson state, and I accept it as recalled, not checked. Third, the SI second has not been redefined. I would not make a scientific prize wait for a CGPM decision, but that decision would remove a reasonable objection if it came before the final ballot. Finally, the instrument-versus-discovery objection (Danielsson, Eriksson) is not answered by saying that the clock is useful. It is answered only to the extent that the clock produced new physical results, and I regard the many-body and redshift results as the evidence that it did.

responses.point: Danielsson prefers IceCube (B021) for Halzen, Spiering and Karle as a discovery that nature supplied and that no one predicted in detail, with the diffuse flux seen in several channels. He ranks the clock fifth because he weighs a measuring invention below a discovery, and he asks whether the pioneers should be recognised while they are alive and active.
responses.response: I take the discovery-versus-instrument distinction seriously, and I find it the best argument against my own preference. My answer is that the flux is firmly established, but what it says about the sources is not yet settled: the origin of the diffuse flux is still largely open, with a few associations (TXS 0506+056, NGC 1068) at modest significance. A prize for a discovery should in my view wait until the explanation is at least in outline. The confirmation is also within IceCube channels, since KM3NeT and Baikal-GVD are not yet at comparable sensitivity, whereas the lattice clock is reproduced across laboratories. The cut among Halzen, Karle and Spiering from a collaboration of hundreds, with DUMAND, Baikal and AMANDA behind it, is a harder allocation than Katori and Ye. I would not exclude B021 in a later year. On the point of living pioneers, I note that both clock laureates and all three IceCube names are alive and active, so I do not see urgency that favours one over the other.

responses.point: Eriksson prefers topological insulators (B016) for Kane, Mele and Molenkamp as a new class of matter defined by topology, with theory and experiment in one prize and fifteen years of confirmation, but he says that B014 is the cleaner configuration if the committee finds the credit gap too large. He also said he agrees B018 is closer to a method than a discovery.
responses.response: I agree that B016 is conceptually the deepest candidate on the list, and I ranked it fifth with that in mind. My difficulty is the one he states himself. Molenkamp's experiment tested a prediction by Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang, who are not among the names, and Zhang's death means the omission cannot be repaired. The 3D work (Fu, Kane, Mele, Moore, Balents, Hasan) is also outside the trio, and the 2016 prize took the topological theme. I do not regard the gap as fatal for Kane and Mele, and I would support B016 if the committee decided originality outweighs tidiness, but I do not think it is cleaner than the clock. In answer to the chair's question to him, the specific fact that would change my view is a credit that includes the HgTe proposal without exceeding three names.

responses.point: Pearce, the chair, moved the lattice clock to the head of his configuration after the opening ballots and says that atomic clocks are outside his expertise, so he relies on Lindroth, Kroll and Johansson for priority history. He records IceCube as his first alternative.
responses.response: I appreciate the disclosure that his position moved, and I agree that agreement reached by members moving toward one candidate counts for less than the arguments behind it, so I have tried to give the arguments only. I would also test the claim that the clock has support from every ranking member, since two of those members rank it fifth. The remaining question for the committee is priority. Since he and I cannot check dates, I would ask that before a final ballot the committee obtains an expert note on the sequence of Katori's proposal, the first strontium lattice demonstrations (including Lemonde and Lisdat) and the 1e-18 comparisons. I do not expect this to change the pair, but we are all recalling the dates, not checking them.

responses.point: Lindroth argues that the lattice clock is a conceptual step and not an incremental improvement, because magic-wavelength trapping controls projection noise and Doppler and recoil shifts together. She disagrees that the committee should wait for the redefinition of the second, and she says the field is close to her own, so she may be too fond of it.
responses.response: Her mechanism argument is the strongest one in the exchange and I use it in my case. I agree with her that a prize for the demonstrated science should not be tied to the CGPM schedule. Where I add a caution is her proximity disclosure: since she is the member who knows the priority history best, the committee should ask her to say which of her statements about priority are checked and which are recalled, instead of treating her disagreement with the sceptics as the check. I would also hold her to the same standard that she applies to B008, that overlap with an earlier prize needs a statable distinction, and I think the citation can state it.

responses.point: Kroll prefers B014 as the clearest case of a new measurement technique opening new observations, and says he should discount his own bias toward metrology. He suggests that B008 (Cirac, Zoller, Blatt) is the natural fallback and asks whether Johansson would support it.
responses.response: I accept his discount of his own bias and I make the same discount for my own first-place ranking of B001. On B008 I ranked it eighth, and I agree with Lindroth and Johansson that much of the ion-gate foundation overlaps with the 2012 prize, so I would not make it the fallback if B014 fails. I would still keep his point that the citation should not promise geodesy and dark-matter searches, since those are mostly projected. A better fallback, in my view, is a prize with a clean theory-plus-experiment pair, which is why I keep B017 in view, with the open pairing mechanism as its weakness.

uncertainties: Exact priority among Katori, Ye, Lemonde, Lisdat, Ludlow, Takamoto and the ion-clock groups. I have not checked the dates and I ask for an expert note.
Whether the committee finds the lattice clock distinct enough from the 2005 and 2012 prizes. I think a citation can state the difference, but others may disagree.
Whether the redefinition of the SI second should come first. I think not, but this is a judgement about timing, not physics.
Whether my own B001 preference is a parochial taste for universality, given that it has no support and that Belavin is missing from the credited names.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict for B014, B001, B017 or B016 is apparent from my profile, and I have no collaboration with any credited candidate. I work in the Gothenburg physics environment together with Goran Johansson and Eva Olsson (Chalmers), who have disclosed proximity to B009 and B042 respectively, and I support the chair's suggestion that they consider stepping back on those parts. Neither is in my preferred configuration. I have no further conflict to add.
